Example 2: Template strand to protein

Problem: The template strand of a short gene reads 3′-TACGGAAAACTTACT-5′. Write the coding strand, the mRNA, and the peptide.

Solution

Coding strand: the complement of the template, written 5′→3′ so it lines up base for base: 5′-ATGCCTTTTGAATGA-3′.

mRNA: RNA polymerase reads the template 3′→5′ and builds the mRNA 5′→3′ as its complement, with U in place of T: 5′-AUG CCU UUU GAA UGA-3′. This is the coding strand with U for T.

Peptide: AUG = Met, CCU = Pro, UUU = Phe, GAA = Glu, UGA = stop: Met-Pro-Phe-Glu.

Check: The template starts 3′-TAC, so the mRNA starts 5′-AUG, the start codon. The coding strand and the mRNA read the same except T/U. Fifteen bases make five codons; the last is a stop, so four amino acids.
597178.note: 1: Example 2, template (3'->5') to coding strand, mRNA and peptide

Example 1: Count the bonds

Problem: Ethanol is oxidized to ethanal (acetaldehyde), and ethanal is oxidized to acetic acid. Use bond counts to show that each step is an oxidation.

Solution

Look only at the carbon that changes (the one bearing the O). Count a C=O double bond as two C–O bonds.

  • Ethanol, CH3CH2OH: the CH2OH carbon has 1 C–O and 2 C–H.
  • Ethanal, CH3CHO: the CHO carbon has 2 C–O (the C=O) and 1 C–H.
  • Acetic acid, CH3COOH: the COOH carbon has 3 C–O (C=O plus C–OH) and 0 C–H.

Ethanol → ethanal: C–O goes from 1 to 2 and C–H from 2 to 1, so it is an oxidation. Ethanal → acetic acid: C–O goes from 2 to 3 and C–H from 1 to 0, another oxidation. Write [O] over each arrow.

Check: The CH3 carbon keeps 3 C–H and 0 C–O the whole way, so it is not part of the change. The acid carbon has no H left, so the chain of oxidations stops there, just as a ketone carbon with no H cannot be oxidized.
597105.note: 3: Example 1 count-the-bonds ethanol -> ethanal -> acetic acid

Example 2: Lysine at three pH values

Problem. Lysine has three groups that can carry a charge: the α-carboxyl group, the α-amino group, and the amino group at the end of its side chain, –(CH2)4NH2. Give the charge on each group and the net charge in strong acid (pH 1), at body pH (7.4), and in strong base (pH 12).

Solution. Use the course rules for each group, then add.

  • pH 1 (strong acid): everything that can be protonated is. α-COOH 0, α-NH3+ +1, side-chain –NH3+ +1. Net +2.
  • pH 7.4 (body pH): carboxyl groups are –COO− and amines are –NH3+. α-COO− −1, α-NH3+ +1, side-chain –NH3+ +1. Net +1.
  • pH 12 (strong base): every group that can lose an H+ has. α-COO− −1, α-NH2 0, side-chain –NH2 0. Net −1.

Check. Charge falls as pH rises (+2 → +1 → −1), and the +1 at pH 7.4 matches the table above for a basic amino acid. Compared with alanine, each answer is one unit more positive in acid and at body pH, because lysine has one extra amine.

Example 3: Combustion with an odd number of O atoms

Problem. Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of butane, C4H10 (lighter fuel).

Solution. Start with C4H10 + O2 → CO2 + H2O and balance C, then H, then O.

  • C: 4 C on the left, so write 4 CO2.
  • H: 10 H on the left, so write 5 H2O.
  • O: the right side now has 4 × 2 + 5 × 1 = 13 O atoms. O2 comes in pairs, so you need 13/2 O2: C4H10 + 13/2 O2 → 4 CO2 + 5 H2O.
  • Clear the fraction: multiply every coefficient by 2.

2 C4H10 + 13 O2 → 8 CO2 + 10 H2O

Check. Left: 8 C, 20 H, 26 O. Right: 8 C, 20 H, 16 + 10 = 26 O. ✓ Any alkane with an even number of carbons gives an odd O count this way, so expect to double.

Example 1: The longest chain goes around the bend

Problem: A student draws CH3CH(CH2CH3)CH2CH3 as a straight four-carbon chain with an ethyl branch on carbon 2 and names it 2-ethylbutane. Find the correct name.

Solution

The name breaks the rule above: an ethyl group on C2 means the chain was not the longest. Circle every end CH3. There are three: the CH3 on the left, the CH3 at the end of the ethyl branch, and the CH3 on the right. Count between each pair:

  • left CH3 to right CH3 (the chain as drawn): 4 carbons;
  • left CH3 to the ethyl CH3: 4 carbons;
  • ethyl CH3 → CH2 → CH → CH2 → right CH3: 5 carbons.

The longest chain turns the corner at the CH and runs through the ethyl branch, so the parent is pentane. The only carbon left over is the left CH3, a methyl branch on the middle carbon, which is C3 from either end. The name is 3-methylpentane.

Check: Both structures have 6 carbons (C6H14), so only the name changed. The correct name has a methyl branch and no ethyl on C2, which agrees with the rule above.

Example 3: An in-frame three-base deletion

Problem: Part of a coding strand reads 5′-…ATC ATC TTT GGT…-3′. A mutation deletes the three bases CTT (the last base of codon 2 and the first two bases of codon 3), giving 5′-…ATC ATT GGT…-3′. Write the codons and amino acids before and after, and classify the mutation.

Solution

Before: mRNA 5′-AUC AUC UUU GGU-3′ = Ile-Ile-Phe-Gly. After: mRNA 5′-AUC AUU GGU-3′ = Ile-Ile-Gly. AUC and AUU both code for Ile, so codon 2 still gives Ile even though its last base changed. The net result is that one amino acid (Phe) is lost and every codon after it is read in the original frame. This is an in-frame deletion, not a frameshift. It is the same change as F508del, the most common cystic fibrosis mutation, which removes one phenylalanine from the CFTR chloride channel; the shortened protein misfolds and is destroyed before it reaches the cell surface.

Check: Twelve bases became nine, a loss of exactly three, so the frame is kept. GGU (Gly) is unchanged after the deletion, which shows the reading frame downstream is intact.

Example 1: Where should the end product act?

Problem: A five-step pathway makes product F: A → B → C → D → E → F, catalyzed by enzymes E1 through E5 in order. The cell has plenty of F. Which enzyme should F inhibit, and why?

Solution

F should inhibit E1, the first committed step. F binds the allosteric site of E1 (negative allosteric control), A stops being turned into B, and the whole pathway shuts off at its start. If F inhibited E5 instead, E1 through E4 would keep running and B, C, D and E would pile up, wasting A and the energy spent making the intermediates. This is feedback inhibition; when F is used up, it leaves E1 and the pathway restarts.

Check: Inhibiting the first step means nothing downstream has anything to work on, so no intermediates accumulate. That matches Figure 11.6.3, where E inhibits enzyme 1.
597171.note: 8: Example 1 feedback inhibition of E1 in A->F pathway

Example 2: Partial versus complete hydrogenation

Problem. A mixed triacylglycerol carries palmitic acid (16:0, no C=C), oleic acid (18:1, one C=C) and linoleic acid (18:2, two C=C). (a) How many moles of H2 are needed to hydrogenate 1 mol of this fat completely, and what is the product? (b) Describe one possible product when only 2 mol of H2 are added.

Solution

Count the C=C bonds: 0 + 1 + 2 = 3. Each C=C uses one H2.

(a) 3 mol H2 per mole of fat (H2, Ni catalyst). Every chain becomes saturated: oleic becomes stearic, linoleic also becomes stearic, and palmitic is unchanged. The product is a triacylglycerol with two stearic chains and one palmitic chain, a solid fat.

(b) With only 2 mol H2, one C=C per mole of fat is left. One possible product: the oleic chain becomes stearic and the linoleic chain loses one of its two C=C, becoming an 18:1 chain. The fat now holds palmitic, stearic and one 18:1 chain: partially hydrogenated, softer than the fully saturated product, and some of the remaining C=C may have been flipped from cis to trans by the catalyst.

Check. 3 C=C at the start; 3 H2 leaves 0 and 2 H2 leaves 1. Palmitic has no C=C and never takes up H2. The glycerol backbone and the three ester bonds are untouched in both cases.
597145.note: 9: Example 2 partial vs complete hydrogenation (3 mol vs 2 mol H2)
